summary: Defines performance metrics for how well GMPLS networks can dynamically set up label switched paths. These measures help compare how quickly and reliably connections can be provisioned. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Like timing how fast and how often a delivery company sets up a new route when you ask for one.

questions: how to measure lsp setup performance
how to measure lsp setup time in gmpls
subtitle: Standard ways to measure how fast, and how reliably, a GMPLS network sets up and tears down label switched paths.

tldr.problem: GMPLS controls very different devices, from routers to optical cross-connects, and they differ drastically in how quickly they can provision connections. Applications and networks need a common way to compare these capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three delay metrics (unidirectional setup, bidirectional setup, graceful release), each with a single-LSP and where relevant a multiple-LSP form, plus sampling procedures using Poisson arrivals and statistics such as minimum, median, maximum, percentile and failure ratio.
tldr.outcome: Implementations and networks can be tested and reported in a consistent way. It is a Proposed Standard that measures the signaling side only; data-path metrics are in a separate document.

today: RFC 5814 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It covers signaling-plane delay only; data-path metrics are defined in a separate document.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) controls many kinds of network elements, including routers, switches, DWDM systems, add-drop multiplexers and photonic or optical cross-connects. These devices differ drastically in dynamic provisioning ability. Adding a control plane to optical circuit switching automates connection provisioning and cuts provisioning delay, so there is growing need to measure it.

This RFC defines metrics and methodologies for the dynamic provisioning performance of GMPLS networks, specifically the performance of the signaling protocol. It builds on the IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) framework in RFC 2330, RFC 2679 and RFC 2681, since LSP setup latency is conceptually similar to round-trip delay. Data-path metrics, such as the time until the forward data path becomes operational, are defined in a separate document.
sections.eli5: Different machines in a phone network are fast or slow at making a new connection. This document is the rulebook for timing them fairly.

sections.title: The Three Core Metrics
sections.content:
Three metrics are defined: unidirectional LSP setup delay, bidirectional LSP setup delay and LSP graceful release delay. Each is first defined as a singleton, one measurement, and later as a sample, a series of measurements.

Each metric lists parameters (such as the ingress and egress LSR IDs ID0 and ID1, and the attempt time T), its units (a real number of milliseconds, or undefined), a definition, discussion, methodology and reporting rules. The setup metrics also have a multiple-LSP form, which sends X Path messages at a Poisson rate Lambda_m after the first one. This captures the case where carriers must set up many LSPs in a short time after a failure, which cannot be deduced from the single-LSP delay.
sections.eli5: There are three stopwatches: one for building a one-way road, one for a two-way road, and one for taking a road down politely. Each can time one road or many roads at once.

sections.title: How Setup Delay Is Measured
sections.content:
For single unidirectional setup, the ingress node ID0 sends the first bit of an RSVP-TE Path message at wire-time T and receives the last bit of the matching Resv message at T+dT. The delay is dT. Since this uses two-way signaling, the ingress and egress clocks need not be synchronized.

The value is undefined, meaning a setup failure, if no Resv arrives within a reasonable period or a PathErr arrives instead. The RFC requires the result to be reported with the chosen upper bound and the route the LSP took. The bidirectional case works the same way but the Path message carries an Upstream Label, and the delay may grow if the downstream node overrides the suggested label.

For the multiple-LSP forms, all LSPs MUST traverse the same route, using Explicit Route Objects or another method such as static configuration. The RFC notes that the upper bound should be chosen carefully because device types vary: some photonic cross-connects must move micro mirrors, which may take several milliseconds, while electronic switches can finish nodal processing within several microseconds.
sections.eli5: You shout "build this road!" and start a stopwatch. When the answer comes back you stop it. If no answer ever comes, or you get "no", you write "failed" instead of a time.

sections.title: Graceful Release and Sampling
sections.content:
The graceful release delay covers two procedures from RFC 3473. When the ingress starts it, it sends a Path message with an Admin Status Object having the Reflect (R) and Delete (D) bits set. The egress answers with a Resv carrying the D bit, or optionally a PathErr with the Path_State_Removed flag, and the ingress then sends a PathTear. The delay runs until the egress receives the last bit of the PathTear. When the egress starts it, it sends a Resv with R and D set. In the ingress-initiated case clock synchronization is required; in the egress-initiated case it is not.

A sample takes many singletons at times drawn from a pseudo-random Poisson process with average rate Lambda between T0 and Tf, following RFC 2330. In active measurement the LSP is released after the holding time Th. Two testing cases are described: with no LSP in the network, which shows the inherent delay of an RSVP-TE implementation, and with a number of LSPs present, which can serve as a scalability metric.
sections.eli5: Taking a road down nicely needs a short chat between both ends first. To get a fair picture, you repeat the test at random times and note every result.

sections.title: Statistics to Report
sections.content:
Given a sample, the RFC defines these statistics:

  • Minimum: undefined values SHOULD be treated as infinitely large, so the minimum is undefined if all values are, or if the sample is empty.
  • Median and percentile: undefined values MUST NOT be included. The X-th percentile is the smallest x for which the empirical distribution function F(x) is at least X.
  • Maximum: undefined values MUST NOT be included, so measurements that exceed the upper bound are not reflected.
  • Failure count: the number of undefined values in a sample.
  • Failure ratio: failure events divided by the sum of valid values and failure events, times 100%.

Five failure types are named: single and multiple unidirectional setup, single and multiple bidirectional setup, and graceful release.
sections.eli5: After many tries you report the fastest, the typical, and the slowest time, and how often it failed. Failed tries do not count as times.

sections.title: Measurement Caveats and Security
sections.content:
The reported delay does not include end-node processing time, and it does not include the ResvConf step of three-way signaling for bidirectional LSPs. The RFC assumes the data plane is installed correctly per RFC 3209 and RFC 3473, and recommends performing the data-path measurements of the companion document as well.

Samples may be gathered actively or passively. Active probing must inject only trivial extra traffic, since too much can skew results and in extreme cases cause congestion and denial of service. Passive collection should not become a way to attack the control plane. If performance data is exposed through SNMP, authentication and rate limiting are advised, and implementers are RECOMMENDED to consider SNMPv3 security features. The security considerations of RSVP and its TE extensions also remain relevant.
sections.eli5: Do not time the delivery trucks so often that you cause a traffic jam yourself, and keep the timing records private.
